'''''Potamogeton perfoliatus''''' ('''claspingleaf pondweed''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=POPE7|taxon=Potamogeton perfoliatus|accessdate=13 October 2015}}</ref>  '''perfoliate pondweed''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''redhead grass'''<ref name=NRCS_factshet>{{cite web |url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/mdpmcfs9988.pdf |title=Claspingleaf pondweed (Potamogeton perfoliatus) Plant Fact Sheet |publisher=USDA-Natural Resources Conservation Service, National Plant Materials Center |date=2010 |author1=Zinecker, E. |author2=West, J. |access-date=February 28, 2017 |archive-date=January 8, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108021227/https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/mdpmcfs9988.pdf }}</ref>) is a perennial aquatic plant in the family [[Potamogetonaceae]] occurring in both standing and flowing freshwater habitats. It is widely distributed globally, occurring in all continents except South America and Antarctica.

==Description==
[[File:PotamogetonPerfoliatus.jpg|thumb|left|Perfoliate pondweed growing in a canal. Note the leaves clasping the stem.]]
Perfoliate pondweed grows from a robust creeping perennial rhizome, intermittently producing round stems up to 3 m long.<ref name='Preston'/> The submerged leaves are oval and translucent, with no stalk, 20–115 mm long and 7–42 mm wide, clasping the stem (perfoliate), a flat apex, and 5–12 veins on either side of the midrib.<ref name='Preston'/> They vary considerably in colour and may be bright green, dark green, yellowish, olive or brownish.<ref name='Preston'/> There are no floating leaves. The [[stipule]]s are rather delicate and usually fall off quite soon after the new leaf has unfurled. The insignificant flowers are produced between June and September.<ref name=Rose/> Fruits are 4 mm across, olive green in colour.

Two subspecies have been described. Subspecies ''perfoliatus'' occurs in the Old World. In North America, populations on the eastern seaboard and the Gulf States are considered to be subsp. ''bupleuroides''.<ref name='Sweden'/> Since many pondweeds, including ''P. perfoliatus'', vary naturally in response to growing conditions,<ref name='Preston'/> it is possible that these variants are ecotypes rather than genuine subspecies. The related ''[[Potamogeton richardsonii|P. richardsonii]]'' was formerly considered a subspecies of ''P. perfoliatus'', but is now classed as a separate species.<ref name='Haynes'/>

Like most other broadleaved pondweeds, perfoliate pondweed is tetraploid, with 2n=52.<ref name=Kap2/>

Over much of its range, perfoliate pondweed is unlikely to be confused with any other pondweed species except perhaps ''P. praelongus''. In North America it could be confused with ''P. richardsonii'', but the latter has stipules that disintegrate to persistent fibres even on the lower part of the stem, whereas those of ''P. perfoliatus'' disintegrate entirely.<ref name='Haynes'/>

However, perfoliate pondweed regularly hybridises with  other ''Potamogeton'' species including ''[[Potamogeton crispus|P. crispus]]'' (''P''. × ''cooperi'' <small>(Fryer) Fryer</small>), ''[[Potamogeton gramineus|P. gramineus]]'' (''P''. × ''nitens'' <small>Weber</small>), ''[[Potamogeton lucens|P. lucens]]'' (''P''. × ''salicifolius'' <small>Wolfg.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton alpinus|P. alpinus]]'' (''P''. × ''prussicus'' <small>Hagstr.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton berchtoldii|P. berchtoldii]]'' (''P''. × ''mysticus'' <small>Morong</small>), ''[[Potamogeton wrightii|P. wrightii]]'' (''P''. × ''anguillanus'' <small>Koidz.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton maackianus|P. maackianus]]'' (''P''. × ''leptocephalus'' <small>Koidz.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton alpinus|P. alpinus]]'' (''P''. × ''prussicus'' <small>Hagstr.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton nodosus|P. nodosus]]'' (''P''. × ''assidens'' <small>Z. Kaplan, Zalewska-Gałosz et M. Ronikier</small>), ''P. richardsonii'' (''P''. × ''absconditus'' <small>Z. Kaplan, Fehrer & Hellq.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton epihydrus|P. epihydrus]]'' (''P.'' × ''versicolor'' <small>Z. Kaplan, Hellq. and Fehrer</small>) and ''[[Potamogeton praelongus|P. praelongus]]'' (''P''. × ''cognatus'' <small>Asch. & Graebn.</small>).<ref name=kwc2/><ref name="Preston"/> The first three of these are quite common.<ref name="Preston"/> A triple hybrid, ''P. gramineus'' × ''lucens'' × ''perfoliatus'' (''P''. × ''torssandrii'' <small>(Tiselius) Dörfler</small>), is also known.<ref name=Kap2/> Many of these hybrids are perennial and long-lived, sometimes occurring in the absence of one or even both parents. Therefore, care should be taken with identification of unusual specimens.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

==Taxonomy==
''Potamogeton perfoliatus'' (perfoliate meaning that the leaf encircles the stem) was one of the original species named by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' (1753).{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

DNA analysis indicates that ''P. perfoliatus'' is one of the broad-leaved pondweed clade (section ''Potamogeton'') and is probably most closely related to [[Potamogeton richardsonii|''P. richardsonii'']].<ref name=Lind/>

==Distribution==
''Potamogeton perfoliatus'' has a broad global distribution, occurring in all continents except South America and Antarctica. It has been recorded from Asia (Afghanistan, India, Indonesia (Sumatra), Japan, Kazakhstan, Korea, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan), Australia,<ref name='Guo'/> North America (Eastern and SE US),<ref name='USDA'/> Europe south to Spain, Central Italy and the Balkans and including Scandinavia, Britain, Ireland and Iceland,<ref name='Sweden'/> North Africa (Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt),<ref name='Sweden'/> the Near and Middle East.  It is widespread in lakes and rivers in the British Isles and Ireland,<ref name=newat/> and is common in much of Eurasia and North America, but has a more scattered distribution towards the southern edge of its range.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

==Ecology and conservation==
''P. perfoliatus'' grows in a wide range of freshwater habitats including lakes, rivers and streams, large ponds, canals and larger drains and ditches. It does not tolerate drying out, and the most robust plants tend to occur in >1 m water depth.<ref name="Preston"/> Unlike most other broad-leaved pondweeds it is reasonably tolerant of water flow and so can use running waters to a significant extent. It is not especially sensitive to water chemistry provided that the water remains reasonably clear and is not too base-poor, occurring in such diverse habitats as exposed Scottish lochs and lowland fenland rivers. However, at high nutrient concentrations it is vulnerable to shading from phytoplankton and epiphytic algae<ref name=Twil/><ref name=Mae/> and filamentous algae.<ref name=Mae/> It may also grow in brackish or estuarine habitats, notably in Chesapeake Bay.<ref name='USDAfact'/><ref name='Caffrey'/> However, elevated salt concentrations have a negative effect on both growth and flowering.<ref name=Brink/>

[[File:Potamogeton perfoliatus bed, Llyn Cregennan Isaf 2014.jpg|thumb|A ''Potamogeton perfoliatus'' bed in Llyn Cregennen Isaf, a high quality lake in Wales (UK)]]

Waterbirds, fish,<ref name='USDAfact'/><ref name=Bra/> water beetles and caddis larvae<ref name=jac/> can all be important grazers of perfoliate pondweed, reducing its biomass or even eliminating it locally.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

Perfoliate pondweed is less threatened than other broadleaved pondweeds, but it is listed as Vulnerable in Spain<ref name=Moreno/> and the Netherlands<ref name=Sparrius/> and Endangered in Flanders.<ref name=INBO/> There are ongoing efforts to restore populations in Chesapeake Bay, where this was formerly a co-dominant species.<ref name=Shaf/><ref name=Hengst/><ref name=Ail/>

[[File:Potamogeton perfoliatus Dordogne.jpg|thumb|''Potamogeton perfoliatus'' in the River Dordogne, France]]
Perfoliate pondweed is the commonest of the so-called ''Magnopotamion'' group of pondweeds. These are a characteristic floristic component of the protected Habitats Directive habitat Type 'Natural eutrophic lakes with ''Magnopotamion''{{'}}.<ref name=JNCC/>

==Cultivation==
Perfoliate pondweed is not widely cultivated, which is perhaps surprising as it is not ecologically demanding and is an attractive plant. In common with other pondweeds of this group it roots poorly from stem cuttings and is best propagated by division of the rhizomes. It is easy to grow in a garden pond or even in a barrel, but unlike some other submerged plants needs to be able to root in a suitable substrate such as sand or aquatic compost. Keeping nutrient levels low helps to prevent smothering by algae and more invasive aquatic plants.<ref name='USDAfact'/> Plants being established should be weighted down initially to allow them to root, and benefit from being planted among other aquatic plants that can act as a 'nursery'.<ref name=Hengst/> Transplants have a high survival rate once established.<ref name=Hengst/>

''P. perfoliatus'' may also be established from seed, which should be sown on a suitable substrate in shallow water. The seed should be left uncovered, or covered only with a minimal amount of substrate to hold the seed in place and allow root development, as seed buried more than 1 cm deep either does not germinate or the seedlings die.<ref name=Ail/> The seed typically germinates within about 10 days.<ref name=Ail/>

Although it is possible to grow perfoliate pondweed in fish ponds, it would be vulnerable to fish predation initially, so should be protected during establishment.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}
